§1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “Moving point-to-point means the times during which an employee is in the process of going to or from a work station. Multi-purpose machine means a machine that is designed to be configured in various ways, at least one of which allows it to hoist (by means of a winch or hook) and horizontally move a suspended load. For example, a machine that can rotate and can be configured with removable forks/tongs (for use as a forklift) or with a winch pack, jib (with a hook at the end) or jib used in conjunction with a winch.”

§1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “Certified welder means a welder who meets nationally recognized certification requirements applicable to the task being performed. Climbing means the process in which a tower crane is raised to a new working height, either by adding additional tower sections to the top of the crane (top climbing), or by a system in which the entire crane is raised inside the structure (inside climbing). Come-a-long means a mechanical device typically consisting of a chain or cable attached at each end that is used to facilitate movement of materials through leverage.” §1926.1400 Scope Coverage starts with power-operated equipment used in construction that can hoist, lower and horizontally move a suspended load. The list includes many crane types, derricks, dedicated pile drivers, service/mechanic trucks with a hoisting device, and variations, and it is not exhaustive [29cfr1926.1400(a)]. Multi-purpose machines are listed when configured to do this with a winch or hook [29cfr1926.1400(a)]. Attachments, whether crane-attached or suspended, don't remove covered equipment from scope [29cfr1926.1400(b)].

Check the exclusions. Machinery converted for non-hoisting use is excluded while so converted [29cfr1926.1400(c)(1)]. Excavators, backhoes, power shovels and listed loaders are excluded even when lifting with rigging [29cfr1926.1400(c)(2)]. Forklifts are excluded except when configured to hoist with a winch or hook and move a suspended load [29cfr1926.1400(c)(8)]. A mechanic's truck is excluded when used in equipment maintenance and repair activities [29cfr1926.1400(c)(9)]. Wreckers, digger derricks, aerial devices, tree work and other listed items also have exclusions, some conditional [29cfr1926.1400(c)]. Digger derrick work under subpart V or telecommunication construction must meet stated compliance conditions to qualify [29cfr1926.1400(c)(4)].

For articulating/knuckle-boom delivery cranes, ground transfer is excluded when materials aren't arranged in a particular sequence for hoisting [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(i)]. Placing building supply sheet goods or packaged materials onto a structure is excluded when using a boom-end fork/cradle, "but only when the truck crane is equipped with a properly functioning automatic overload prevention device" [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(ii)]. The exclusion doesn't apply when holding, supporting or stabilizing material to facilitate construction [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(iii)(A)], or when handling prefabricated components [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(iii)(B)] or structural steel members or systems-engineered metal building components [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(iii)(C)].

Employers must establish, effectively communicate and enforce work rules ensuring compliance with provisions directing employee actions [29cfr1926.1400(f)]. Controlling entity duties include those in the sections named in [29cfr1926.1400(e)]. “industrial cranes (such as carry-deck cranes); dedicated pile drivers; service/mechanic trucks with a hoisting device; a crane on a monorail; tower cranes (such as a fixed jib, i.e., “hammerhead boom”), luffing boom and self-erecting); pedestal cranes; portal cranes; overhead and gantry cranes; straddle cranes; sideboom cranes; derricks; and variations of such equipment. However, items listed in paragraph (c) of this section are excluded from the scope of this standard. (b) Attachments. This standard applies to equipment included in paragraph (a) of this section when used with attachments.”

body.text: §1926.1401 Definitions

These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401].

Boatswain's chair means a single-point adjustable suspension scaffold consisting of a seat or sling (which may be incorporated into a full body harness) designed to support one employee in a sitting position. Bogie means “travel bogie,” which is defined below. Boom (equipment other than tower crane) means an inclined spar, strut, or other long structural member which supports the upper hoisting tackle on a crane or derrick. Typically, the length and vertical angle of the boom can be varied to achieve increased height or height and reach when lifting loads.
§1926.1432 Multiple-crane/derrick lifts—supplemental requirements

These supplemental requirements apply to a crane/derrick operation in which more than one crane/derrick will be supporting the load. The operation must be planned before it begins [29cfr1926.1432(a)].

For the plan itself, a qualified person must develop it [29cfr1926.1432(a)(1)]. It must be designed "to ensure that the requirements of this subpart are met" [29cfr1926.1432(a)(2)]. For implementation, the lift must be directed by a lift director, and there are two acceptable arrangements [29cfr1926.1432(b)(1)]. The first is a single person who meets the criteria for both a competent person and a qualified person. The second is a competent person "who is assisted by one or more qualified persons" [29cfr1926.1432(b)(1)]. Under the wording of that paragraph, a competent person who does not also meet the qualified person criteria needs that assistance to fit either arrangement.

The lift director must also review the plan in a meeting with all workers who will be involved with the operation [29cfr1926.1432(b)(2)].

§1926.1400 Scope Coverage starts with power-operated equipment used in construction that can hoist, lower and horizontally move a suspended load. The list includes many crane types, derricks, dedicated pile drivers, service/mechanic trucks with a hoisting device, and variations, and it is not exhaustive [29cfr1926.1400(a)]. Multi-purpose machines are listed when configured to do this with a winch or hook [29cfr1926.1400(a)]. Attachments, whether crane-attached or suspended, don't remove covered equipment from scope [29cfr1926.1400(b)].

Check the exclusions. Machinery converted for non-hoisting use is excluded while so converted [29cfr1926.1400(c)(1)]. Excavators, backhoes, power shovels and listed loaders are excluded even when lifting with rigging [29cfr1926.1400(c)(2)]. Forklifts are excluded except when configured to hoist with a winch or hook and move a suspended load [29cfr1926.1400(c)(8)]. A mechanic's truck is excluded when used in equipment maintenance and repair activities [29cfr1926.1400(c)(9)]. Wreckers, digger derricks, aerial devices, tree work and other listed items also have exclusions, some conditional [29cfr1926.1400(c)]. Digger derrick work under subpart V or telecommunication construction must meet stated compliance conditions to qualify [29cfr1926.1400(c)(4)].

For articulating/knuckle-boom delivery cranes, ground transfer is excluded when materials aren't arranged in a particular sequence for hoisting [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(i)]. Placing building supply sheet goods or packaged materials onto a structure is excluded when using a boom-end fork/cradle, "but only when the truck crane is equipped with a properly functioning automatic overload prevention device" [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(ii)]. The exclusion doesn't apply when holding, supporting or stabilizing material to facilitate construction [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(iii)(A)], or when handling prefabricated components [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(iii)(B)] or structural steel members or systems-engineered metal building components [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(iii)(C)].

Employers must establish, effectively communicate and enforce work rules ensuring compliance with provisions directing employee actions [29cfr1926.1400(f)]. Controlling entity duties include those in the sections named in [29cfr1926.1400(e)]. “industrial cranes (such as carry-deck cranes); dedicated pile drivers; service/mechanic trucks with a hoisting device; a crane on a monorail; tower cranes (such as a fixed jib, i.e., “hammerhead boom”), luffing boom and self-erecting); pedestal cranes; portal cranes; overhead and gantry cranes; straddle cranes; sideboom cranes; derricks; and variations of such equipment. However, items listed in paragraph (c) of this section are excluded from the scope of this standard.” §1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “§ 1926.1401 Definitions. A/D director (Assembly/Disassembly director) means an individual who meets this subpart's requirements for an A/D director, irrespective of the person's formal job title or whether the person is non-management or management personnel. Articulating crane means a crane whose boom consists of a series of folding, pin connected structural members, typically manipulated to extend or retract by power from hydraulic cylinders. Assembly/Disassembly means the assembly and/or disassembly of equipment covered under this standard.”

§1926.1402 Ground conditions Do not assemble or use the equipment unless the ground is firm, drained and graded enough to meet the manufacturer's specifications for adequate support and degree of level. You may count supporting materials, if necessary, toward meeting them. Drainage is not required in marshes or wetlands [29cfr1926.1402(b)]. Ground conditions include slope, compaction and firmness [29cfr1926.1402(a)(1)]. Supporting materials include blocking, mats, cribbing, marsh buggies in marshes or wetlands, and similar materials or devices [29cfr1926.1402(a)(2)].

The controlling entity must ensure the necessary ground preparations are provided [29cfr1926.1402(c)(1)]. It must also inform the equipment user and operator of the location of hazards beneath the set-up area, such as voids, tanks and utilities. The duty covers hazards identified in documents in its possession, on or off site, or hazards it otherwise knows about [29cfr1926.1402(c)(2)].

Without a controlling entity, the preparation duty in (c)(1) falls on the employer with authority at the site to make or arrange the preparations [29cfr1926.1402(d)].

If you, as operator, or the A/D director determine that conditions fall short, that person's employer must discuss the needed preparations with the controlling entity. The aim is to meet paragraph (b), using suitable supporting materials or devices if necessary [29cfr1926.1402(e)]. A limited exclusion applies to certain cranes on railroad tracks [29cfr1926.1402(f)]. “(c) The controlling entity must: (1) Ensure that ground preparations necessary to meet the requirements in paragraph (b) of this section are provided. (2) Inform the user of the equipment and the operator of the location of hazards beneath the equipment set-up area (such as voids, tanks, utilities) if those hazards are identified in documents (such as site drawings, as-built drawings, and soil analyses) that are in the possession of the controlling entity (whether at the site or off-site) or the hazards are otherwise known to that controlling entity.” §1926.1411 Power line safety—while traveling under or near power lines with no load These procedures and criteria cover equipment traveling with no load under or near a power line on a construction site. Loaded travel falls under § 1926.1408, § 1926.1409 or § 1926.1410, whichever is appropriate, and § 1926.1417(u) [29cfr1926.1411(a)].

The employer must ensure the boom/mast and its support system are lowered sufficiently [29cfr1926.1411(b)(1)], Table T clearances are maintained [29cfr1926.1411(b)(2)], and speed and terrain effects, including boom/mast movement, are considered so they do not cause a breach of minimum clearance [29cfr1926.1411(b)(3)].

Table T minimums, by nominal AC voltage in kV, are: up to 0.75, 4 feet; over .75 to 50, 6 feet; over 50 to 345, 10 feet; over 345 to 750, 16 feet; over 750 to 1,000, 20 feet. Over 1,000, the distance is established by the utility owner/operator or a registered professional engineer qualified in electrical power transmission and distribution [29cfr1926.1411-table-T].

If any part of traveling equipment will get closer than 20 feet to the line, a dedicated spotter in continuous contact with you is required [29cfr1926.1411(b)(4)]. The spotter must be positioned to gauge clearance effectively, use direct communication equipment where necessary, and give you "timely information" so clearance can be maintained [29cfr1926.1411(b)(4)].

At night or in poor visibility, lines must also be illuminated or otherwise located, and a safe travel path identified and used [29cfr1926.1411(b)(5)]. “(i) The power lines are illuminated or another means of identifying the location of the lines is used. (ii) A safe path of travel is identified and used. §1926.1404 Assembly/Disassembly—general requirements (applies to all assembly and disassembly operations) Assembly/disassembly is directed by the A/D director: a competent and qualified person, or a competent person assisted by qualified persons. A lone worker must be both [29cfr1926.1404(a)]. The director must understand the procedures [29cfr1926.1404(b)], reviewing them immediately beforehand unless already understanding and having applied them to the same equipment type and configuration [29cfr1926.1404(c)]. Crew must understand tasks, hazards and locations to avoid before work, task changes or additions of personnel [29cfr1926.1404(d)].

Crew must notify you before entering covered out-of-view locations where equipment or load movement could injure them [29cfr1926.1404(e)(1)]. If you know someone went there, move no part or load until the pre-arranged communication system confirms they are safe [29cfr1926.1404(e)(2)]. Nobody may be under components during pin removal unless the employer demonstrates site constraints require it; the director must then minimize movement risk and exposure [29cfr1926.1404(f)].

Rated capacity limits apply in all phases [29cfr1926.1404(g)]. The director addresses ground, blocking, assist crane loads (verified beforehand), pick points, center of gravity, stability at pin removal, snagging, counterweights, backward stability and weather [29cfr1926.1404(h)]. Test the boom hoist brake each time before relying on it; if insufficient, use another specified protection against boom movement [29cfr1926.1404(h)(10)].

Observe manufacturer cantilever limits, or if unavailable, a registered professional engineer's written limit [29cfr1926.1404(j)]. Keep component weights readily available [29cfr1926.1404(k)]. Components and configuration affecting capacity or safety follow manufacturer requirements (or written engineer approval if unavailable) or qualifying approved modifications; inspect after assembly [29cfr1926.1404(m)]. Remove and safely stow reusable shipping hardware [29cfr1926.1404(o)]. No jib during pile driving [29cfr1926.1404(p)].

Whenever outriggers or stabilizers are required or used, rules cover extension, floats, visibility and blocking; outriggers, except on locomotive cranes, must take equipment weight off wheels. Locomotive cranes have manufacturer-procedure rules [29cfr1926.1404(q)]. Rigging requires a qualified rigger, synthetic sling protection and compliance with sling manufacturer instructions and recommendations, alongside other applicable rigging standards [29cfr1926.1404(r)]. “For purposes of this standard, that person is considered the A/D director. (b) Knowledge of procedures. The A/D director must understand the applicable assembly/disassembly procedures. (c) Review of procedures. The A/D director must review the applicable assembly/disassembly procedures immediately prior to the commencement of assembly/disassembly unless the A/D director understands the procedures and has applied them to the same type and configuration of equipment (including accessories, if any).” §1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “§ 1926.1401 Definitions. A/D director (Assembly/Disassembly director) means an individual who meets this subpart's requirements for an A/D director, irrespective of the person's formal job title or whether the person is non-management or management personnel. Articulating crane means a crane whose boom consists of a series of folding, pin connected structural members, typically manipulated to extend or retract by power from hydraulic cylinders.”

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “Assist crane means a crane used to assist in assembling or disassembling a crane. Attachments means any device that expands the range of tasks that can be done by the equipment. Examples include, but are not limited to: An auger, drill, magnet, pile-driver, and boom-attached personnel platform. Audible signal means a signal made by a distinct sound or series of sounds. Examples include, but are not limited to, sounds made by a bell, horn, or whistle. Blocking (also referred to as “cribbing”) is wood or other material used to support equipment or a component and distribute loads to the ground.” Appendix B to Subpart CC of Part 1926 Appendix B to Subpart CC of Part 1926—Assembly/Disassembly: Sample Procedures for Minimizing the Risk of Unintended Dangerous Boom Movement For pin removal, the appendix cites § 1926.1404(f)(1): employees must not be under the boom, jib, or other components unless § 1926.1404(f)(2) is met. That exception applies when the employer demonstrates that site constraints require one or more employees to be there. The A/D director must then implement procedures that "minimize the risk of unintended dangerous movement and minimize the duration and extent of exposure under the boom" [29cfr1926.cc.appB].

In the sample, aboveground piping prevents lowering the boom, and the aerial lift, based on the near side, cannot be repositioned, so its basket must go under the boom. A rigged assist crane supports the detaching section, with particular care that the end near the pin removers is well supported. Far side pins come out first, the basket returns to the near side as soon as possible, then near side pins come out [29cfr1926.cc.appB].

During assembly/disassembly, the load's center of gravity must be identified if the stability method requires it. With insufficient information, measures must prevent unintended dangerous movement from misidentifying it. In the sample, the director cannot determine the pick point above a non-symmetrical top section's center of gravity. With personnel clear, it is raised a few inches to check for tipping. If it tips, the hoist line is repositioned and the test repeated until the director determines it can be moved without dangerous movement [29cfr1926.cc.appB]. “To minimize the risk of unintended dangerous movement while the pins are removed, the A/D director uses an assist crane that is rigged to support the boom section that is being detached, using particular care to ensure that the section end that is near the employee(s) removing the pins is well supported. The duration and extent of exposure is minimized by removing the far side pins first, moving the aerial lift basket as soon as possible to the near side so that the employees are no longer under the boom, and then removing the near side pins.”

Appendix B to Subpart CC of Part 1926 Appendix B to Subpart CC of Part 1926—Assembly/Disassembly: Sample Procedures for Minimizing the Risk of Unintended Dangerous Boom Movement

For pin removal, the appendix cites § 1926.1404(f)(1): employees must not be under the boom, jib, or other components unless § 1926.1404(f)(2) is met. That exception applies when the employer demonstrates that site constraints require one or more employees to be there. The A/D director must then implement procedures that "minimize the risk of unintended dangerous movement and minimize the duration and extent of exposure under the boom" [29cfr1926.cc.appB].

In the sample, aboveground piping prevents lowering the boom, and the aerial lift, based on the near side, cannot be repositioned, so its basket must go under the boom. A rigged assist crane supports the detaching section, with particular care that the end near the pin removers is well supported. Far side pins come out first, the basket returns to the near side as soon as possible, then near side pins come out [29cfr1926.cc.appB].

During assembly/disassembly, the load's center of gravity must be identified if the stability method requires it. With insufficient information, measures must prevent unintended dangerous movement from misidentifying it. In the sample, the director cannot determine the pick point above a non-symmetrical top section's center of gravity. With personnel clear, it is raised a few inches to check for tipping. If it tips, the hoist line is repositioned and the test repeated until the director determines it can be moved without dangerous movement [29cfr1926.cc.appB].

To minimize the risk of unintended dangerous movement while the pins are removed, the A/D director uses an assist crane that is rigged to support the boom section that is being detached, using particular care to ensure that the section end that is near the employee(s) removing the pins is well supported. The duration and extent of exposure is minimized by removing the far side pins first, moving the aerial lift basket as soon as possible to the near side so that the employees are no longer under the boom, and then removing the near side pins.

§1926.1410(d)(2)(iv) “(iv) Give timely information to the operator so that the required clearance distance can be maintained.” §1926.1410 Power line safety (all voltages)—equipment operations closer than the Table A zone Operating inside the § 1926.1408 Table A distance is prohibited unless the employer demonstrates that all conditions are met [29cfr1926.1410]. The employer must determine that breaching it is unavoidable for feasibility reasons [29cfr1926.1410(a)] and, after consulting the utility, that deenergizing and grounding or relocating the line is infeasible [29cfr1926.1410(b)]. The line owner/operator or a qualified registered professional engineer sets the minimum clearance [29cfr1926.1410(c)(1)]; subpart V work uses employer-established § 1926.960(c)(1)(i) distances [29cfr1926.1410(c)(2)].

Planned procedures [29cfr1926.1410(d)] include disabling automatic reclosing before work, if design permits [29cfr1926.1410(d)(1)]; a continuously connected, well-positioned spotter with a visual aid, giving timely information, with direct communication equipment where necessary [29cfr1926.1410(d)(2)]; and a flagged or similarly marked elevated warning line or barricade, unattached to the crane and visible to you directly or by video [29cfr1926.1410(d)(3)]. An insulating link goes between the load line end (or below) and load [29cfr1926.1410(d)(4)(i)]. Subpart V is excepted from both. Link substitutes ran only until November 8, 2011 [29cfr1926.1410(d)(4)(iv)] and November 8, 2013 [29cfr1926.1410(d)(4)(v)].

Rigging that may enter the Table A distance, and any tag line, must be nonconductive [29cfr1926.1410(d)(5)] [29cfr1926.1410(d)(7)]. Any range limiter must be used and set to protect the established clearance [29cfr1926.1410(d)(6)]. Perimeter barricades are at least 10 feet out, or as far as feasible where obstructed [29cfr1926.1410(d)(8)]. Others may not touch the crane or the load line above the link; remote ground operators need isolating wireless controls or insulating mats [29cfr1926.1410(d)(9)]. Only essential personnel stay near [29cfr1926.1410(d)(10)]. Ground the equipment [29cfr1926.1410(d)(11)]. The utility installs line hose or cover-up unless unavailable for the voltage [29cfr1926.1410(d)(12)].

Procedures are documented, reviewed and implemented [29cfr1926.1410(e)] [29cfr1926.1410(f)] [29cfr1926.1410(g)]. One director has stop-work authority [29cfr1926.1410(h)]. Problems or inadequacy require safely stopping; before resuming, develop new procedures or have the utility deenergize and visibly ground, or relocate, the line [29cfr1926.1410(j)]. Safety devices and aids follow manufacturer conditions [29cfr1926.1410(k)]. Training follows § 1926.1408(g) [29cfr1926.1410(m)]. “§ 1926.1410 Power line safety (all voltages)—equipment operations closer than the Table A zone.”

§1926.1410 Power line safety (all voltages)—equipment operations closer than the Table A zone

Operating inside the § 1926.1408 Table A distance is prohibited unless the employer demonstrates that all conditions are met [29cfr1926.1410]. The employer must determine that breaching it is unavoidable for feasibility reasons [29cfr1926.1410(a)] and, after consulting the utility, that deenergizing and grounding or relocating the line is infeasible [29cfr1926.1410(b)]. The line owner/operator or a qualified registered professional engineer sets the minimum clearance [29cfr1926.1410(c)(1)]; subpart V work uses employer-established § 1926.960(c)(1)(i) distances [29cfr1926.1410(c)(2)].

Planned procedures [29cfr1926.1410(d)] include disabling automatic reclosing before work, if design permits [29cfr1926.1410(d)(1)]; a continuously connected, well-positioned spotter with a visual aid, giving timely information, with direct communication equipment where necessary [29cfr1926.1410(d)(2)]; and a flagged or similarly marked elevated warning line or barricade, unattached to the crane and visible to you directly or by video [29cfr1926.1410(d)(3)]. An insulating link goes between the load line end (or below) and load [29cfr1926.1410(d)(4)(i)]. Subpart V is excepted from both. Link substitutes ran only until November 8, 2011 [29cfr1926.1410(d)(4)(iv)] and November 8, 2013 [29cfr1926.1410(d)(4)(v)].

Rigging that may enter the Table A distance, and any tag line, must be nonconductive [29cfr1926.1410(d)(5)] [29cfr1926.1410(d)(7)]. Any range limiter must be used and set to protect the established clearance [29cfr1926.1410(d)(6)]. Perimeter barricades are at least 10 feet out, or as far as feasible where obstructed [29cfr1926.1410(d)(8)]. Others may not touch the crane or the load line above the link; remote ground operators need isolating wireless controls or insulating mats [29cfr1926.1410(d)(9)]. Only essential personnel stay near [29cfr1926.1410(d)(10)]. Ground the equipment [29cfr1926.1410(d)(11)]. The utility installs line hose or cover-up unless unavailable for the voltage [29cfr1926.1410(d)(12)].

Procedures are documented, reviewed and implemented [29cfr1926.1410(e)] [29cfr1926.1410(f)] [29cfr1926.1410(g)]. One director has stop-work authority [29cfr1926.1410(h)]. Problems or inadequacy require safely stopping; before resuming, develop new procedures or have the utility deenergize and visibly ground, or relocate, the line [29cfr1926.1410(j)]. Safety devices and aids follow manufacturer conditions [29cfr1926.1410(k)]. Training follows § 1926.1408(g) [29cfr1926.1410(m)].

§1926.1435(e)(5)(ii) Boom hoist limiting device “(ii) Boom hoist limiting device. The range of the boom must be limited at the minimum and maximum radius. Temporary alternative measures: Clearly mark the cable (so it can be seen by the operator) at a point that will give the operator sufficient time to stop the boom hoist within the minimum and maximum boom radius, or use a spotter who is in direct communication with the operator to inform the operator when this point is reached.” §1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “With regard to tower cranes, “erecting and climbing” replaces the term “assembly,” and “dismantling” replaces the term “disassembly.” Regardless of whether the crane is initially erected to its full height or is climbed in stages, the process of increasing the height of the crane is an erection process. Assist crane means a crane used to assist in assembling or disassembling a crane. Attachments means any device that expands the range of tasks that can be done by the equipment. Examples include, but are not limited to: An auger, drill, magnet, pile-driver, and boom-attached personnel platform.”

body.text: §1926.1401 Definitions

These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

§1926.1414(e)(3) “(3) When Types II and III with an operating design factor of less than 5 are used (for non-duty cycle, non-repetitive lifts), the following requirements must be met for each lifting operation: (i) A qualified person must inspect the rope in accordance with § 1926.1413(a). The rope must be used only if the qualified person determines that there are no deficiencies constituting a hazard. In making this determination, more than one broken wire in any one rope lay must be considered a hazard.” §1926.1414 Wire rope—selection and installation criteria Original and replacement rope must be selected and installed under this section. Replacement selection follows the rope manufacturer's, equipment manufacturer's, or a qualified person's recommendations [29cfr1926.1414(a)]. Rope must be compatible with safe equipment functioning [29cfr1926.1414(c)]. Non-rotation-resistant rope must meet ASME B30.5-2004 section 5-1.7.1, excluding paragraph (c) [29cfr1926.1414(b)(1)], or the performance option tied to rated capacity and § 1926.1413 inspections [29cfr1926.1414(b)(2)].

Rotation resistant types are Type I (at least 15 outer strands, at least three layers), Type II (at least 10, two or more layers) and Type III (no more than nine, two layers) [29cfr1926.1414(e)(1)]. The operating design factor floor for all is 3.5 [29cfr1926.1414(e)(2)(ii)]. Type I needs at least 5 unless both the rope and equipment manufacturers approve the factor in writing [29cfr1926.1414(e)(2)(iii)]. Types II and III below 5 are barred from duty cycle or repetitive lifts [29cfr1926.1414(e)(2)(i)]. For other lifts below 5, each operation requires a qualified person's inspection under § 1926.1413(a), with use only if no hazardous deficiencies are found; more than one broken wire in any one rope lay is a hazard [29cfr1926.1414(e)(3)(i)]. Operating manner and speed must minimize dynamic effects [29cfr1926.1414(e)(3)(ii)]. Record each such lift in the monthly and annual inspection documents; the qualified person considers prior uses before reuse [29cfr1926.1414(e)(3)(iii)].

For boom hoists, fiber core rope is allowed only on derricks [29cfr1926.1414(d)(1)]. Rotation resistant rope is allowed only where load hoists act as boom hoists for attachments such as luffing or boom and mast systems. Drum first-layer and all sheave pitch diameters must be at least 18 times nominal rope diameter, the system design factor at least five, and the other listed conditions met, including any power-controlled lowering system's capability [29cfr1926.1414(e)(4)(ii)].

Wedge socket clips attach only to the unloaded dead end, though purpose-designed dead-ending devices are permitted [29cfr1926.1414(f)]. Socket as the rope or fitting manufacturer specifies [29cfr1926.1414(g)]. response.text:
§1926.1420 Signals—radio, telephone or other electronic transmission of signals When signals go by radio, telephone or another electronic method, three requirements apply [29cfr1926.1420].

Testing comes first. The devices used to transmit signals must be tested on site before operations begin. The purpose is to ensure that transmission is "effective, clear, and reliable" [29cfr1926.1420(a)]. The text places this test both at the site and ahead of the start of operations.

Next is the channel. Signal transmission must use a dedicated channel unless an exception applies [29cfr1926.1420(b)]. Under the first, multiple cranes or derricks and one or more signal persons "may share a dedicated channel for the purpose of coordinating operations" [29cfr1926.1420(b)(1)]. This permits sharing for that purpose, and the channel being shared is still described as dedicated.

The second exception concerns a crane operating on or adjacent to railroad tracks, where the crane operator's actions need to be coordinated with the movement of other equipment or trains on the same or adjacent tracks [29cfr1926.1420(b)(2)]. Both the location and the need for coordination are part of its wording.

Finally, the way you receive signals as operator is specified: reception "must be by a hands-free system" [29cfr1926.1420(c)]. “§ 1926.1420 Signals—radio, telephone or other electronic transmission of signals. (a) The device(s) used to transmit signals must be tested on site before beginning operations to ensure that the signal transmission is effective, clear, and reliable. (b) Signal transmission must be through a dedicated channel, except: (1) Multiple cranes/derricks and one or more signal persons may share a dedicated channel for the purpose of coordinating operations.”

§1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “Articulating crane means a crane whose boom consists of a series of folding, pin connected structural members, typically manipulated to extend or retract by power from hydraulic cylinders. Assembly/Disassembly means the assembly and/or disassembly of equipment covered under this standard. With regard to tower cranes, “erecting and climbing” replaces the term “assembly,” and “dismantling” replaces the term “disassembly.” Regardless of whether the crane is initially erected to its full height or is climbed in stages, the process of increasing the height of the crane is an erection process.”

response.text: §1926.1423(b)(2) Boom walkway criteria “(2) Boom walkway criteria. (i) The walkways must be at least 12 inches wide. (ii) Guardrails, railings and other permanent fall protection attachments along walkways are: (A) Not required. (B) Prohibited on booms supported by pendant ropes or bars if the guardrails/railings/attachments could be snagged by the ropes or bars. (C) Prohibited if of the removable type (designed to be installed and removed each time the boom is assembled/disassembled). (D) Where not prohibited, guardrails or railings may be of any height up to, but not more than, 45 inches.” §1926.1423(b) Boom walkways “(b) Boom walkways. (1) Equipment manufactured after November 8, 2011 with lattice booms must be equipped with walkways on the boom(s) if the vertical profile of the boom (from cord centerline to cord centerline) is 6 or more feet. (2) Boom walkway criteria. (i) The walkways must be at least 12 inches wide. (ii) Guardrails, railings and other permanent fall protection attachments along walkways are: (A) Not required.”

§1926.1417 Operation Follow applicable manufacturer procedures; where unavailable, the employer's substitutes apply [29cfr1926.1417(a)] [29cfr1926.1417(b)(1)]. Keep procedures and load charts in the cab; if electronic-only capacities become inaccessible, cease operations or follow safe shut-down until available [29cfr1926.1417(c)]. Avoid diverting activities while operating [29cfr1926.1417(d)].

Leaving controls under a suspended load requires all of these: you stay adjacent without other duties; the hold exceeds normal lifting time; the competent person finds it safe and restrains specified functions; and barricades or caution lines, plus notices, keep all employees out of the fall zone [29cfr1926.1417(e)(1)]. Negligible-weight working gear not over an entrance or exit is excepted [29cfr1926.1417(e)(2)].

With warning signs, don't start or activate the affected control until an authorized person removes the sign, or you verify nobody is servicing, working on or dangerously positioned on the machine, and it is repaired and working properly [29cfr1926.1417(f)(2)]. Before engine start, verify control positions and clear personnel [29cfr1926.1417(g)]. Promptly report needed repairs in writing to the designated person and any next-shift operator [29cfr1926.1417(j)(1)].

Stay within rated capacity [29cfr1926.1417(o)(1)]. Verify load weight through recognized or equally reliable information, provided before the lift on request. Alternatively, begin hoisting with a listed device to check whether it exceeds 75 percent of maximum rated capacity at the longest radius to be used; if so, don't proceed until weight is verified by the first method [29cfr1926.1417(o)(3)].

At 90% or more of maximum line pull, lift a few inches and apply brakes each time; in duty-cycle or repetitive lifts all at that level, test only the first [29cfr1926.1417(s)]. Keep at least two full wraps on drums [29cfr1926.1417(t)].

No obstruction contact, side dragging or pulling, or front-area lifts on wheeled equipment unless the manufacturer permits [29cfr1926.1417(p)] [29cfr1926.1417(q)] [29cfr1926.1417(r)]. Control swing and load rotation, adjust brakes properly, and obey anyone's stop signal [29cfr1926.1417(v)] [29cfr1926.1417(w)] [29cfr1926.1417(x)] [29cfr1926.1417(y)]. Travel, slack-rope, wind/ice/snow, locomotive-crane and counterweight conditions also apply [29cfr1926.1417(u)] [29cfr1926.1417(m)] [29cfr1926.1417(n)] [29cfr1926.1417(z)] [29cfr1926.1417(aa)]. Safety devices and aids don't replace judgment [29cfr1926.1417(k)]. “(x) The brakes must be adjusted in accordance with manufacturer procedures to prevent unintended movement. (y) The operator must obey a stop (or emergency stop) signal, irrespective of who gives it. (z) Swinging locomotive cranes. A locomotive crane must not be swung into a position where railway cars on an adjacent track could strike it, until it is determined that cars are not being moved on the adjacent track and that proper flag protection has been established. (aa) Counterweight/ballast.”

§1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “See Upperworks. Tagline means a rope (usually fiber) attached to a lifted load for purposes of controlling load spinning and pendular motions or used to stabilize a bucket or magnet during material handling operations. Tender means an individual responsible for monitoring and communicating with a diver. Tilt up or tilt down operation means raising/lowering a load from the horizontal to vertical or vertical to horizontal. Tower crane is a type of lifting structure which utilizes a vertical mast or tower to support a working boom (jib) in an elevated position.”

response.text:
Appendix C to Subpart CC of Part 1926 Appendix C to Subpart CC of Part 1926—Operator Certification: Written Examination: Technical Knowledge Criteria Appendix C gives information to those developing criteria for a written test of an operator's technical knowledge of crane operation [29cfr1926.cc.appC]. It states no numeric limits. Its topics relate to daily work as follows.

Technical topics include crane and attachment limitations [29cfr1926.cc.appC(a)(1)], wire rope capacity, line pull and selection [29cfr1926.cc.appC(a)(2)], rigging devices [29cfr1926.cc.appC(a)(3)], limits of electrical protective measures and proximity to power lines, radii and microwave structures [29cfr1926.cc.appC(a)(4)], and multi-crane load share and transfer [29cfr1926.cc.appC(a)(5)]. Others include power flow systems [29cfr1926.cc.appC(a)(7)], instruments [29cfr1926.cc.appC(a)(8)], safety devices and operational aids [29cfr1926.cc.appC(a)(11)], net capacity for every possible configuration [29cfr1926.cc.appC(a)(13)], load dimensions, weight and center of gravity [29cfr1926.cc.appC(a)(15)], dynamic and side loading, and backward stability [29cfr1926.cc.appC(a)].

Site topics cover ground support, mats, cribbing and supports, hazards, plan reviews (including working height, boom length, load radius and travel clearance), and room to extend crawlers, outriggers or stabilizers, and counterweights [29cfr1926.cc.appC(b)].

Operating topics include load handling, communication, reeving, changing conditions, shutdown, weather, leveling, verifying weights and radii, basic rigging and shift inspection [29cfr1926.cc.appC(c)]. Operations such as personnel hoisting, pile driving or work on water are identified as requiring "specific procedures and skill levels" [29cfr1926.cc.appC(c)(12)]. Safe procedures are listed for conditions including traveling with suspended loads, power lines, reduced outrigger, crawler or stabilizer extension, and blind lifts [29cfr1926.cc.appC(c)(13)]. Load control, tag lines, emergencies such as overload or control malfunction, and outrigger use also appear [29cfr1926.cc.appC(c)].

Load chart topics include choosing the appropriate chart, footnote limitations, configuration, structural versus stability limits, range diagrams, work area charts, "parts-of-line" information, and use with load indicators and/or load moment devices [29cfr1926.cc.appC(d)]. “(12) The difference between duty-cycle and lifting operations. (13) How to calculate net capacity for every possible configuration of the equipment using the manufacturer's load chart. (14) How to use manufacturer-approved attachments and their effect on the equipment. (15) How to obtain dimensions, weight, and center of gravity of the load. (16) The effects of dynamic loading from: (i) Wind. (ii) Stopping and starting. (iii) Impact loading. (iv) Moving with the load. (17) The effect of side loading. (18) The principles of backward stability. (b) Site information.”

Others include power flow systems [29cfr1926.cc.appC(a)(7)], instruments [29cfr1926.cc.appC(a)(8)], safety devices and operational aids [29cfr1926.cc.appC(a)(11)], net capacity for every possible configuration [29cfr1926.cc.appC(a)(13)], load dimensions, weight and center of gravity [29cfr1926.cc.appC(a)(15)], dynamic and side loading, and backward stability [29cfr1926.cc.appC(a)].

Site topics cover ground support, mats, cribbing and supports, hazards, plan reviews (including working height, boom length, load radius and travel clearance), and room to extend crawlers, outriggers or stabilizers, and counterweights [29cfr1926.cc.appC(b)].

Operating topics include load handling, communication, reeving, changing conditions, shutdown, weather, leveling, verifying weights and radii, basic rigging and shift inspection [29cfr1926.cc.appC(c)]. Operations such as personnel hoisting, pile driving or work on water are identified as requiring "specific procedures and skill levels" [29cfr1926.cc.appC(c)(12)]. Safe procedures are listed for conditions including traveling with suspended loads, power lines, reduced outrigger, crawler or stabilizer extension, and blind lifts [29cfr1926.cc.appC(c)(13)]. Load control, tag lines, emergencies such as overload or control malfunction, and outrigger use also appear [29cfr1926.cc.appC(c)].

Load chart topics include choosing the appropriate chart, footnote limitations, configuration, structural versus stability limits, range diagrams, work area charts, "parts-of-line" information, and use with load indicators and/or load moment devices [29cfr1926.cc.appC(d)].

(12) The difference between duty-cycle and lifting operations. (13) How to calculate net capacity for every possible configuration of the equipment using the manufacturer's load chart. (14) How to use manufacturer-approved attachments and their effect on the equipment. (15) How to obtain dimensions, weight, and center of gravity of the load. (16) The effects of dynamic loading from: (i) Wind. (ii) Stopping and starting. (iii) Impact loading. (iv) Moving with the load. (17) The effect of side loading. (18) The principles of backward stability. (b) Site information.

Appendix C to Subpart CC of Part 1926 (a)(4)(iii) “(iii) Insulated links.” §1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “Hoist means a mechanical device for lifting and lowering loads by winding a line onto or off a drum. §1926.1438(b)(1) “(1) This paragraph applies to the following equipment when used in construction and not permanently installed in a facility: Overhead and gantry cranes, overhead/bridge cranes, semigantry, cantilever gantry, wall cranes, storage bridge cranes, launching gantry cranes, and similar equipment having the same fundamental characteristics, irrespective of whether it travels on tracks, wheels, or other means.” §1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “Such devices do not include boatswain's chairs when hoisted by equipment covered by this standard. Marine worksite means a construction worksite located in, on or above the water. Mobile crane means a lifting device incorporating a cable suspended latticed boom or hydraulic telescopic boom designed to be moved between operating locations by transport over the road. Moving point-to-point means the times during which an employee is in the process of going to or from a work station.” §1926.1438(a) Permanently installed overhead and gantry cranes “(a) Permanently installed overhead and gantry cranes. The requirements of § 1910.179, except for § 1910.179(b)(1), and not the requirements of this subpart CC, apply to the following equipment when used in construction and permanently installed in a facility: overhead and gantry cranes, including semigantry, cantilever gantry, wall cranes, storage bridge cranes, and others having the same fundamental characteristics.”

body.text: §1926.1438 Overhead & gantry cranes

For overhead and gantry cranes used in construction, permanent installation in a facility decides the rule set. Permanently installed equipment follows § 1910.179, except paragraph (b)(1), and not subpart CC. This includes semigantry, cantilever gantry, wall, storage bridge and similar cranes [29cfr1926.1438(a)].

Equipment not permanently installed also includes overhead/bridge and launching gantry cranes, however it travels [29cfr1926.1438(b)(1)]. It must meet these:

First, §§ 1926.1400 through 1926.1414, 1926.1417 through 1926.1425, 1926.1426(d), 1926.1427 through 1926.1434, 1926.1437, 1926.1439 and 1926.1441 [29cfr1926.1438(b)(2)(i)].

Second, selected provisions within paragraphs (b), (e), (f) and (h) of § 1910.179, plus paragraphs (g), (k) and (n) [29cfr1926.1438(b)(2)(ii)(A)].

Third, the definitions in § 1910.179(a). For "hoist" and "load," however, use § 1926.1401 [29cfr1926.1438(b)(2)(ii)(B)].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. response.text:
§1910.179 Overhead and gantry cranes Only designated personnel operate [29cfr1910.179(b)(8)]. Stay within rated load except for tests [29cfr1910.179(n)(1)]; test loads are limited to 125 percent unless the manufacturer recommends otherwise [29cfr1910.179(k)(2)]. Each shift, try every upper hoist limit under no load, inching or slowly; immediately notify the appointed person of faults. Never use it as an operating control [29cfr1910.179(n)(4)].

Check rope, lines and hook position before hoisting; secure and balance loads; avoid sudden speed changes and obstructions. Side pulls need specific authorization. No movement with employees on load or hook. Avoid carrying loads over people, test brakes near rated load, keep two full drum wraps, stay at controls, and sound warnings when required. Multi-crane lifts need one qualified responsible person in charge [29cfr1910.179(n)(3)].

Frequent inspections run daily to monthly, periodic 1 to 12 months [29cfr1910.179(j)(1)(ii)]. Hooks and chains need daily visual and monthly certified checks; hook limits are over 15 percent excess throat opening or over 10° twist [29cfr1910.179(j)(2)]. Idle 1 to under 6 months requires frequent and idle-rope inspection; over 6 months, complete and idle-rope inspection; standby cranes, frequent and idle-rope inspection at least semi-annually [29cfr1910.179(j)(4)]. Running ropes need monthly certified inspection; ropes idle a month or more need appointed-person approval [29cfr1910.179(m)].

Before repair, position the crane, turn controllers off, lock the main or emergency switch open, post signs and protect against other cranes [29cfr1910.179(l)(2)(i)].

Equipment limits: ANSI B30.2.0-1967 design for new cranes from August 31, 1971 [29cfr1910.179(b)(2)]; clearances 3 inches overhead, 2 lateral, 3 around cabs; access gaps 12 inches (30 cm) maximum [29cfr1910.179(b)(6)(i)] [29cfr1910.179(c)]; footwalk headroom 48 inches, load design 50 pounds per square foot [29cfr1910.179(d)]; steppable guards support 200 pounds [29cfr1910.179(e)(6)(iii)]. Bumpers, subject to exceptions: bridge 3 ft/s/s at 20 percent rated speed, 40 percent energy capacity; trolley 4.7 at one-third [29cfr1910.179(e)]. Holding torque: 125 percent with nonmechanical control braking, 100 with mechanical, 100 each for two [29cfr1910.179(f)(2)(i)]. Foot force maximum 70 pounds; stopping feet equal 10 percent of full-load feet-per-minute speed [29cfr1910.179(f)(4)]. Voltage: control 600, pendant 150 AC/300 DC, cab-crane receptacle 300 [29cfr1910.179(g)]. Rope load per part: 20 percent breaking strength; retighten new-rope clips after one hour [29cfr1910.179(h)(2)]. “(iv) The wearing surface of all brakedrums or discs shall be smooth. (v) All foot-brake pedals shall be constructed so that the operator's foot will not easily slip off the pedal.
