§1926.1404 Assembly/Disassembly—general requirements (applies to all assembly and disassembly operations) Assembly/disassembly is directed by the A/D director: a competent and qualified person, or a competent person assisted by qualified persons. A lone worker must be both [29cfr1926.1404(a)]. The director must understand the procedures [29cfr1926.1404(b)], reviewing them immediately beforehand unless already understanding and having applied them to the same equipment type and configuration [29cfr1926.1404(c)]. Crew must understand tasks, hazards and locations to avoid before work, task changes or additions of personnel [29cfr1926.1404(d)].

Crew must notify you before entering covered out-of-view locations where equipment or load movement could injure them [29cfr1926.1404(e)(1)]. If you know someone went there, move no part or load until the pre-arranged communication system confirms they are safe [29cfr1926.1404(e)(2)]. Nobody may be under components during pin removal unless the employer demonstrates site constraints require it; the director must then minimize movement risk and exposure [29cfr1926.1404(f)].

Rated capacity limits apply in all phases [29cfr1926.1404(g)]. The director addresses ground, blocking, assist crane loads (verified beforehand), pick points, center of gravity, stability at pin removal, snagging, counterweights, backward stability and weather [29cfr1926.1404(h)]. Test the boom hoist brake each time before relying on it; if insufficient, use another specified protection against boom movement [29cfr1926.1404(h)(10)].

Observe manufacturer cantilever limits, or if unavailable, a registered professional engineer's written limit [29cfr1926.1404(j)]. Keep component weights readily available [29cfr1926.1404(k)]. Components and configuration affecting capacity or safety follow manufacturer requirements (or written engineer approval if unavailable) or qualifying approved modifications; inspect after assembly [29cfr1926.1404(m)]. Remove and safely stow reusable shipping hardware [29cfr1926.1404(o)]. No jib during pile driving [29cfr1926.1404(p)].

Whenever outriggers or stabilizers are required or used, rules cover extension, floats, visibility and blocking; outriggers, except on locomotive cranes, must take equipment weight off wheels. Locomotive cranes have manufacturer-procedure rules [29cfr1926.1404(q)]. Rigging requires a qualified rigger, synthetic sling protection and compliance with sling manufacturer instructions and recommendations, alongside other applicable rigging standards [29cfr1926.1404(r)]. “(i) Protect the structural integrity of the equipment, and (ii) Prevent dangerous movement and collapse. (4) Verifying assist crane loads. When using an assist crane, the loads that will be imposed on the assist crane at each phase of assembly/disassembly must be verified in accordance with § 1926.1417(o)(3) before assembly/disassembly begins. (5) Boom and jib pick points. The point(s) of attachment of rigging to a boom (or boom sections or jib or jib sections) must be suitable for preventing structural damage and facilitating safe handling of these components.” §1926.1417 Operation Follow applicable manufacturer procedures; where unavailable, the employer's substitutes apply [29cfr1926.1417(a)] [29cfr1926.1417(b)(1)]. Keep procedures and load charts in the cab; if electronic-only capacities become inaccessible, cease operations or follow safe shut-down until available [29cfr1926.1417(c)]. Avoid diverting activities while operating [29cfr1926.1417(d)].

Leaving controls under a suspended load requires all of these: you stay adjacent without other duties; the hold exceeds normal lifting time; the competent person finds it safe and restrains specified functions; and barricades or caution lines, plus notices, keep all employees out of the fall zone [29cfr1926.1417(e)(1)]. Negligible-weight working gear not over an entrance or exit is excepted [29cfr1926.1417(e)(2)].

With warning signs, don't start or activate the affected control until an authorized person removes the sign, or you verify nobody is servicing, working on or dangerously positioned on the machine, and it is repaired and working properly [29cfr1926.1417(f)(2)]. Before engine start, verify control positions and clear personnel [29cfr1926.1417(g)]. Promptly report needed repairs in writing to the designated person and any next-shift operator [29cfr1926.1417(j)(1)].

Stay within rated capacity [29cfr1926.1417(o)(1)]. Verify load weight through recognized or equally reliable information, provided before the lift on request. Alternatively, begin hoisting with a listed device to check whether it exceeds 75 percent of maximum rated capacity at the longest radius to be used; if so, don't proceed until weight is verified by the first method [29cfr1926.1417(o)(3)].

At 90% or more of maximum line pull, lift a few inches and apply brakes each time; in duty-cycle or repetitive lifts all at that level, test only the first [29cfr1926.1417(s)]. Keep at least two full wraps on drums [29cfr1926.1417(t)].

No obstruction contact, side dragging or pulling, or front-area lifts on wheeled equipment unless the manufacturer permits [29cfr1926.1417(p)] [29cfr1926.1417(q)] [29cfr1926.1417(r)]. Control swing and load rotation, adjust brakes properly, and obey anyone's stop signal [29cfr1926.1417(v)] [29cfr1926.1417(w)] [29cfr1926.1417(x)] [29cfr1926.1417(y)]. Travel, slack-rope, wind/ice/snow, locomotive-crane and counterweight conditions also apply [29cfr1926.1417(u)] [29cfr1926.1417(m)] [29cfr1926.1417(n)] [29cfr1926.1417(z)] [29cfr1926.1417(aa)]. Safety devices and aids don't replace judgment [29cfr1926.1417(k)]. “(p) The boom or other parts of the equipment must not contact any obstruction. (q) The equipment must not be used to drag or pull loads sideways. (r) On wheel-mounted equipment, no loads must be lifted over the front area, except as permitted by the manufacturer. (s) The operator must test the brakes each time a load that is 90% or more of the maximum line pull is handled by lifting the load a few inches and applying the brakes. In duty cycle and repetitive lifts where each lift is 90% or more of the maximum line pull, this requirement applies to the first lift but not to successive lifts.”

With warning signs, don't start or activate the affected control until an authorized person removes the sign, or you verify nobody is servicing, working on or dangerously positioned on the machine, and it is repaired and working properly [29cfr1926.1417(f)(2)]. Before engine start, verify control positions and clear personnel [29cfr1926.1417(g)]. Promptly report needed repairs in writing to the designated person and any next-shift operator [29cfr1926.1417(j)(1)].

Stay within rated capacity [29cfr1926.1417(o)(1)]. Verify load weight through recognized or equally reliable information, provided before the lift on request. Alternatively, begin hoisting with a listed device to check whether it exceeds 75 percent of maximum rated capacity at the longest radius to be used; if so, don't proceed until weight is verified by the first method [29cfr1926.1417(o)(3)].

No obstruction contact, side dragging or pulling, or front-area lifts on wheeled equipment unless the manufacturer permits [29cfr1926.1417(p)] [29cfr1926.1417(q)] [29cfr1926.1417(r)]. Control swing and load rotation, adjust brakes properly, and obey anyone's stop signal [29cfr1926.1417(v)] [29cfr1926.1417(w)] [29cfr1926.1417(x)] [29cfr1926.1417(y)]. Travel, slack-rope, wind/ice/snow, locomotive-crane and counterweight conditions also apply [29cfr1926.1417(u)] [29cfr1926.1417(m)] [29cfr1926.1417(n)] [29cfr1926.1417(z)] [29cfr1926.1417(aa)]. Safety devices and aids don't replace judgment [29cfr1926.1417(k)].

(p) The boom or other parts of the equipment must not contact any obstruction. (q) The equipment must not be used to drag or pull loads sideways. (r) On wheel-mounted equipment, no loads must be lifted over the front area, except as permitted by the manufacturer. (s) The operator must test the brakes each time a load that is 90% or more of the maximum line pull is handled by lifting the load a few inches and applying the brakes. §1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “Marine worksite means a construction worksite located in, on or above the water. Mobile crane means a lifting device incorporating a cable suspended latticed boom or hydraulic telescopic boom designed to be moved between operating locations by transport over the road. Moving point-to-point means the times during which an employee is in the process of going to or from a work station. Multi-purpose machine means a machine that is designed to be configured in various ways, at least one of which allows it to hoist (by means of a winch or hook) and horizontally move a suspended load.”

§1910.180 Crawler locomotive and truck cranes Only designated personnel operate [29cfr1910.180(b)(3)]. Design: ANSI B30.5-1968 for new cranes from August 31, 1971; older cranes "should be modified" by February 15, 1972, subject to an exception [29cfr1910.180(b)(2)]. Maximum ratings (% of tipping): locomotive without outriggers, 85 (booms 60 feet or less, and over), with a 30,000 pound-feet minimum net stabilizing moment; locomotive, outriggers fully extended, 80; crawler without, 75, extended, 85; truck/wheel, without or extended, 85 [29cfr1910.180-table-1]. Locomotive rating track is within 1 percent grade [29cfr1910.180(c)(1)(ii)(b)]. Account for wind, ground, tires, speeds and other stability factors [29cfr1910.180(c)(1)(iv)]. Keep the chart visible from your seat [29cfr1910.180(c)(2)].

Exceed rated load only for testing [29cfr1910.180(h)(1)(i)]; tests stop at 110 percent [29cfr1910.180(e)(2)(ii)]. Structurally limited loads need weight known within ±10 percent [29cfr1910.180(h)(1)(ii)]. Sling loads; never wrap the hoist rope around them [29cfr1910.180(h)(2)]. Level, block, balance and control movement; no sideways dragging or riders [29cfr1910.180(h)(3)]. Test brakes by raising near-rated loads a few inches [29cfr1910.180(h)(3)(viii)]. Use outriggers when load exceeds the no-outrigger rating [29cfr1910.180(h)(3)(ix)]. Keep two full drum wraps [29cfr1910.180(h)(3)(x)]. Multiple-crane lifts and loaded travel need a designated person [29cfr1910.180(h)(3)(xii)] [29cfr1910.180(h)(3)(xiv)]. Stay at controls under suspended loads [29cfr1910.180(h)(4)(i)].

Inspect new or altered cranes before use [29cfr1910.180(d)(1)]. Frequent: daily to monthly; periodic: 1 to 12 months or manufacturer's recommendation [29cfr1910.180(d)(2)]. Control maladjustment and air/hydraulic checks are daily [29cfr1910.180(d)(3)]. Hook criteria are cracks, throat over 15 percent excess, or twist over 10°; the sentence omits the action [29cfr1910.180(d)(3)(v)]. Idle one month to under 6 needs frequent and idle-rope checks; six months adds periodic; standby gets the former at least semiannually [29cfr1910.180(d)(5)]. Certify critical items and ropes monthly [29cfr1910.180(d)(6)] [29cfr1910.180(g)(1)]. Ropes idle a month or more need approval before reuse [29cfr1910.180(g)(2)(ii)]. Reinstate guards and safety devices, and remove maintenance equipment, before operating [29cfr1910.180(f)]. Never refuel running [29cfr1910.180(i)(4)(ii)]. “§ 1910.180 Crawler locomotive and truck cranes. (a) Definitions applicable to this section. (1) A crawler crane consists of a rotating superstructure with power plant, operating machinery, and boom, mounted on a base, equipped with crawler treads for travel.”

With regard to tower cranes, “erecting and climbing” replaces the term “assembly,” and “dismantling” replaces the term “disassembly.”

Examples include, but are not limited to: An auger, drill, magnet, pile-driver, and boom-attached personnel platform.

§1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

§1926.1414 Wire rope—selection and installation criteria Original and replacement rope must be selected and installed under this section. Replacement selection follows the rope manufacturer's, equipment manufacturer's, or a qualified person's recommendations [29cfr1926.1414(a)]. Rope must be compatible with safe equipment functioning [29cfr1926.1414(c)]. Non-rotation-resistant rope must meet ASME B30.5-2004 section 5-1.7.1, excluding paragraph (c) [29cfr1926.1414(b)(1)], or the performance option tied to rated capacity and § 1926.1413 inspections [29cfr1926.1414(b)(2)].

Rotation resistant types are Type I (at least 15 outer strands, at least three layers), Type II (at least 10, two or more layers) and Type III (no more than nine, two layers) [29cfr1926.1414(e)(1)]. The operating design factor floor for all is 3.5 [29cfr1926.1414(e)(2)(ii)]. Type I needs at least 5 unless both the rope and equipment manufacturers approve the factor in writing [29cfr1926.1414(e)(2)(iii)]. Types II and III below 5 are barred from duty cycle or repetitive lifts [29cfr1926.1414(e)(2)(i)]. For other lifts below 5, each operation requires a qualified person's inspection under § 1926.1413(a), with use only if no hazardous deficiencies are found; more than one broken wire in any one rope lay is a hazard [29cfr1926.1414(e)(3)(i)]. Operating manner and speed must minimize dynamic effects [29cfr1926.1414(e)(3)(ii)]. Record each such lift in the monthly and annual inspection documents; the qualified person considers prior uses before reuse [29cfr1926.1414(e)(3)(iii)].

For boom hoists, fiber core rope is allowed only on derricks [29cfr1926.1414(d)(1)]. Rotation resistant rope is allowed only where load hoists act as boom hoists for attachments such as luffing or boom and mast systems. Drum first-layer and all sheave pitch diameters must be at least 18 times nominal rope diameter, the system design factor at least five, and the other listed conditions met, including any power-controlled lowering system's capability [29cfr1926.1414(e)(4)(ii)].

Wedge socket clips attach only to the unloaded dead end, though purpose-designed dead-ending devices are permitted [29cfr1926.1414(f)]. Socket as the rope or fitting manufacturer specifies [29cfr1926.1414(g)]. Before cutting, seize both sides, following the rope manufacturer's length and number instructions [29cfr1926.1414(h)]. “(c) Wire rope must be compatible with the safe functioning of the equipment. (d) Boom hoist reeving. (1) Fiber core ropes must not be used for boom hoist reeving, except for derricks. (2) Rotation resistant ropes must be used for boom hoist reeving only where the requirements of paragraph (e)(4)(ii) of this section are met. (e) Rotation resistant ropes— (1) Definitions— (i) Type I rotation resistant wire rope (“Type I”). Type I rotation resistant rope is stranded rope constructed to have little or no tendency to rotate or, if guided, transmits little or no torque.”

§1926.1437 Floating cranes/derricks and land cranes/derricks on barges This supplements the subpart for floating and barge-mounted cranes and derricks, excluding jacked barges fully supported by deployed jacks [29cfr1926.1437(a)]. Work area control applies except § 1926.1424(a)(2)(ii); use barriers, or signs plus equipment markings and employee training [29cfr1926.1437(c)]. § 1926.1425 doesn't apply [29cfr1926.1437(d)]. Add list/trim and house-lock devices, plus a wind indicator when a competent person finds wind relevant [29cfr1926.1437(e)]. Anti two-block applies only to personnel hoisting or hoisting over occupied cofferdams or shafts; listed work has load-weighing relief [29cfr1926.1437(f)]. Cab or no-cab information-access rules apply [29cfr1926.1437(g)].

Competent persons inspect the flotation each shift and monthly [29cfr1926.1437(h)(3)]. Annual external and four-year internal inspections require specified expertise; hazards remove the vessel from service, and flagged nonhazards are monitored [29cfr1926.1437(h)(4)] [29cfr1926.1437(h)(5)]. Document monthly, annual and four-year inspections; keep four-year records at least 4 years [29cfr1926.1437(h)(6)].

Diver work requires dedicated crane use until all divers return, continuous control attendance, tender sightline or electronic signals, and no-shift securing [29cfr1926.1437(j)]. Don't exceed vessel environmental, operating or transit limits [29cfr1926.1437(k)].

For permanent marine equipment, follow water charts and their parameters; charts consider minimum 40 mph wind [29cfr1926.1437(m)(1)]. List/trim maximums, in degrees, are 5 each at 25 tons or less, 7 over 25, and 10 for derricks [29cfr1926.1437-table-M1]. Stability: 60 mph with 2 ft freeboard at rated capacity or high boom/no load; 1 ft at capacity plus 25% [29cfr1926.1437-table-M2]; backward stability, high boom/no load/full back list, 90 mph [29cfr1926.1437-table-M3]. Employer-made equipment needs engineer-signed proof [29cfr1926.1437(m)(4)].

Land equipment needs expert derating [29cfr1926.1437(n)(2)]. Vessel list/trim cannot exceed the least of 5 degrees or the manufacturer's limit (qualified person's if unspecified), and must preserve above-water decks and a fully submerged bottom [29cfr1926.1437(n)(3)(i)] [29cfr1926.1437(n)(4)]. Crane list/trim limits also apply [29cfr1926.1437(n)(3)(ii)]. Secure by attachment, corral, rails or centerline cable, except qualifying mobile auxiliaries under a plan [29cfr1926.1437(n)]. Both equipment categories have hull requirements [29cfr1926.1437(m)(5)] [29cfr1926.1437(n)(7)]. “| | Any rated capacity | 10 | 10 (3) The employer must ensure that the equipment is stable under the conditions specified in Tables M2 and M3 of this section. §1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “Electrical contact occurs when a person, object, or equipment makes contact or comes in close proximity with an energized conductor or equipment that allows the passage of current. Employer-made equipment means floating cranes/derricks designed and built by an employer for the employer's own use. Encroachment is where any part of the crane, load line or load (including rigging and lifting accessories) breaches a minimum clearance distance that this subpart requires to be maintained from a power line. Equipment means equipment covered by this subpart.”

§1926.1427 Operator training, certification, and evaluation Covered equipment requires training, certification or licensing, and evaluation; otherwise, you operate only as a supervised trainee [29cfr1926.1427(a)(1)]. Derricks, sidebooms and equipment rated 2,000 pounds or less are excepted, but their training rules remain [29cfr1926.1427(a)(2)]. Military qualifications are employer-specific and last as the issuer stipulates [29cfr1926.1427(a)(3)].

Trainees need formal and practical instruction, assigned tasks within their ability, and continuous on-site monitoring by a qualified employer employee or agent doing nothing distracting [29cfr1926.1427(b)]. Non-tower cranes require line of sight plus verbal or hand signals; tower cranes require direct communication. Breaks are limited to 15 minutes, one per hour, after a task-and-limits briefing, with tasks within ability [29cfr1926.1427(b)(4)]. Uncertified trainees cannot work where equipment, line or load at maximum radius could reach within 20 feet of power lines up to 350 kV, or 50 feet above that voltage. They also cannot hoist personnel, make multiple-equipment lifts, or work over shafts or cofferdams or in tank farms. Multiple-lift rigging is barred unless the trainer finds their skills sufficient [29cfr1926.1427(b)(3)].

Qualifying state or local licensing governs within its jurisdiction (maximum validity 5 years); otherwise certification is required, with no employee cost [29cfr1926.1427(c)]. Accredited certification is type-based or type-and-capacity-based, portable among employers required to use that option, and valid 5 years; accreditation review occurs at least every 3 years [29cfr1926.1427(d)]. Audited-employer certification lasts 5 years and is not portable [29cfr1926.1427(e)(6)]. Audits occur within 3 months of program start, then at least every 3 years [29cfr1926.1427(e)(3)]. Significant deficiencies halt qualification until confirmed correction, require re-audit within 180 days afterward and an auditor's OSHA report within 15 days of determination; auditors keep audit records 3 years [29cfr1926.1427(e)(5)].

Evaluation covers safe operation, equipment-specific features and assigned hoisting [29cfr1926.1427(f)(1)]. Other equipment is allowed if the employer can demonstrate no substantially different abilities are needed [29cfr1926.1427(f)(5)]. Performance or knowledge evaluation indicating a need triggers retraining and subject re-evaluation [29cfr1926.1427(b)(5)] [29cfr1926.1427(f)(7)]. Pre-December 10, 2018 employees may be covered by prior assessments [29cfr1926.1427(f)(2)]. The section's effective date is December 10, 2018; evaluation and documentation, February 7, 2019 [29cfr1926.1427(k)]. “(iii) The government authority that oversees the licensing department/office has determined that the requirements in paragraphs (c)(1)(i) and (ii) of this section have been met. (iv) The licensing department/office has testing procedures for re-licensing designed to ensure that the operator continues to meet the technical knowledge and skills requirements in paragraphs (j)(1) and (2) of this section. (v) For the purposes of compliance with this section, a license is valid for the period of time stipulated by the licensing department/office, but no longer than 5 years. (2) Certification.”
